function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository, followed by a short “how‑to” guide that walks you through the remaining Git steps (add, commit, push).  
The files are written with the assumption that the application is a simple Express/Node.js service that listens on port **3000**.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the Node.js runtime.  
> * Installing dependencies before copying the source code allows Docker to cache the `npm ci` step, speeding up rebuilds.  
> * The container exposes port 3000, which matches the default Express port used in the repo.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML

Using the provided helper function, we generate a deployment and service file.  
(If you prefer to write it manually, the content below is the same.)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to change?**  
> * Replace `yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name/tag you will push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> * If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port`/`targetPort` as needed.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI – Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repository
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or GitHub Container Registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker tag yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Push the image to Docker Hub
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push yourdockerhub/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password).  
> If you prefer GitHub Container Registry, replace the login step with `docker/login-action@v3` using `registry: ghcr.io` and adjust the image names accordingly.

---

## 4. Add, Commit, and Push

Open a terminal in the repository root and run:

```bash
# Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

> **Tip:**  
> If you’re using a fork or a different branch, replace `main` with the appropriate branch name.

---

### Recap

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Clone `git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` |
| 2 | Add `Dockerfile`, `k8s.yaml`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| 3 | Stage, commit, and push the changes |
| 4 | The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and push a Docker image whenever you push to `main` |

Once the workflow completes, you can pull the image from your registry and deploy it to any Kubernetes cluster using the provided YAML. Happy coding!
